newsitem.title: JAPAN: Monetary policy to stress basis for recovery -- BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Monetary policy to stress basis for recovery -- BOJ.

text.p: The monetary policy of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will continue to put emphasis on strengthening the basis for economic recovery while the central bank keeps close watch on developments in the economy, BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference on Wednesday.
"Our monetary policy for now is to make the basis for economic recovery more solid," he said, adding that the central bank would keep watch on economic developments.
"The economy is continuing its gradual recovery and the recovery is becoming more solid," he said.

Despite a fall in public works spending, net exports were continuing to rise and housing investment remained at a high level. Private consumption was gradually strengthening, as seen in strong car sales.
Corporate capital spending was gradually growing and various surveys showed that companies' spending plans for the next fiscal year were "relatively solid" considering the time of year, he said.
In this environment, companies were maintaining increased production, Matsushita said.
He said it seemed that increases in corporate profits and income were supporting private consumption, which was leading to a boost in production.
Despite a decline in public works spending, a positive cyclical mechanism was at work, he said. "This is very encouraging when looking at future prospects," Matsushita said.

He said it was "inevitable" that the economy would temporarily slow down due to fiscal tightening measures such as the increase in the consumption tax. "But the cyclical mechanism has been strengthening recently and the trend of economic recovery is likely to continue."
He added that the central bank still needed to confirm this trend by looking at economic data, the views of the market and companies' business plans.
A decline in prices had come to a halt with improvements in domestic supply and demand conditions and a rise in import prices, he said.
He said he did not think rising prices of imports were likely to put more upward pressure on domestic prices, but said the BOJ would like to keep close watch on domestic prices.

Asked about the recent rise in Japan's trade surplus, he said: "For now, there is a high possibility that the current account surplus will stay on an increasing trend as the effect of the weaker yen will linger and economic growth abroad will continue."

But imports would continue to increase due to structural changes in which Japanese companies had set up manufacturing bases overseas, and also because the ability of East Asian nations to supply more goods to Japan was strengthening.
He said the trend of economic recovery in Japan would continue. "So the pace of increase in the current account surplus overall will stay gradual."

The scheduled rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1 had in the short term boosted demand ahead of implementation and would dampen demand afterwards, he said. In the long term it might affect consumers' purchasing habits, he said.

As for the short-term effect, strong car sales may be partly attributable to the imminent rise in the tax, and there was likely to be some negative effect after April 1. But he said many people held the view that the short-term effect would not be as marked as when Japan introduced the tax.
"The short-term effect may be mild," he said.
But the BOJ would like to keep watch on the longer-term effect on consumer sentiment to see what impact it had on consumer spending habits, he said.
